summary: A genus of flowering vines native to Latin America and the Caribbean. Its climbing members have distinctive three-pronged, hooked tendrils.
An order of green algae in Chlorophyta, with no native origin stated in the supplied sources. It is the only order in its class.
A fern species native from the Canary Islands through Europe, northern Africa and western Asia to the western Himalayas. It is the sole species in its genus.
A plant genus in the dogbane family, containing one species listed for Madagascar and another for South Africa.

A freshwater red-alga genus widespread across the Northern Hemisphere, despite being green in colour. Its stiff, coarse-hair-like strands may be branched or unbranched and have small swellings at intervals.

A genus of thread-forming green algae found mostly in soil and on moist surfaces, although aquatic species and one marine species are known. It forms unbranched, one-cell-wide threads of cylindrical or barrel-shaped cells.

A mostly freshwater green-alga genus with a worldwide distribution, found in still or flowing water and most commonly during colder months. Its unbranched, one-cell-wide threads have cells with two overlapping, H-shaped wall halves.

A flowering shrub or small tree native to eastern and western Africa, including Madagascar. Its drooping, angular branches bear spines, and male and female flowers usually grow on separate plants, although they may occur on one plant.

A flowering vine originating in tropical South America and Central America, perennial where the climate is frost-free. It has highly fragrant, multicoloured flowers with distinctive corkscrew-like shapes.
edibilityNote: Seeds could be edible, but parts of the plant might be poisonous.

summary: A cactus tribe found mostly in the tropical forests of Central and northern South America. Most members climb or grow on other plants, and their diverse flowers range from large white night-opening blooms to bright red daytime blooms.
A plant tribe from Southeast Asia and Oceania, with its main centre of diversity in Australia.

A tuberous begonia hybrid group derived primarily from high-altitude Latin American species. The plants die back to dormant tubers in winter and regrow, producing showy flowers in almost every colour except blue on forms ranging from trailing to upright.

A medium-sized artificial hybrid tree of uncertain origin that arose in Germany around 1818. It has dull red flower clusters and coarse, dark leaves, and is fertile enough to produce viable seeds whose offspring closely resemble the parent.
An ornamental flowering plant native to North Africa. It is the sole species in its genus, is cultivated in gardens and also grows as a weed in California.
A genus of red algae with 11 currently accepted species.
A flowering hybrid created from two species native to the Canary Islands. It can be raised from seed and is grown under cool conditions with protection from frost.

A one-species genus of flowering trees whose sole member, Curtisia dentata, is an evergreen native to South Africa. That species has dark glossy foliage and long-lasting white berries; harvesting its medicinal bark has contributed to declines in some areas, and the tree is protected in South Africa.

A genus of annual or perennial herbs and small woody shrubs found from southern and eastern Europe and northwestern Africa across Asia to the Himalayas and Altai Mountains. Its aromatic leaves and preference for open, often dry habitats are characteristic.

A widespread genus of freshwater green algae found floating in ponds and lakes or living on the bottom in mires and swamps. Its cells often form colonies that repeatedly double in number within a conspicuous, sometimes layered jelly-like envelope.

A possibly single-species genus of succulents native to Namaqualand in Namibia and South Africa’s Cape Provinces. Its rounded leaf tips have transparent windows, and wild plants commonly remain buried in sand except for these tips.

A deciduous willow hybrid native to Europe and western Asia, especially riversides and wetlands. Its twigs snap cleanly with an audible crack, while broken branches can root after waterways carry them downstream.

A genus of succulent flowering plants endemic to South Africa’s Cape Provinces. Its species have pairs of thick, grey-green, pitted leaves resembling split pebbles, with disproportionately large flowers emerging between them.

A subfamily of flowering aquatic plants that floats on or just below still or slow-moving fresh water. Duckweeds lack obvious stems and leaves; their simple bodies may have no roots or several rootlets and reproduce mainly by budding.
edibilityNote: Consumed in Laos, Thailand and Myanmar, used in place of salads or vegetables, and cultivated as a vegetable in Israel.

summary: A genus of bromeliads whose species are endemic to humid tropical and subtropical Brazil. Their flower clusters have a distinctive nest-like form.
A genus of flowering bromeliads native only to eastern Brazil. Its species grow on rocky outcrops and are generally giant bromeliads that collect substantial rainwater between their leaf bases.
A genus of orchids native to Costa Rica, Panama, Venezuela, Colombia, Ecuador and Peru. Each swollen stem bears one leaf, and the flowers resemble pansies.

A plant hybrid between Kalanchoe daigremontiana and Kalanchoe delagoensis. Its leaves are relatively narrow, with bases ranging from tapered or wedge-shaped to weakly heart-shaped or eared; of its four forms, only form A is considered invasive.
A flowering-plant hybrid native to mainland Portugal.

A genus of about 57 subtropical succulent species native to South Africa, especially Cape Province and the Karoo. Its plants have thick, soft paired leaves held near the ground and produce narrow-petalled yellow flowers in autumn and winter, sometimes with fragrance.

An intergeneric orchid hybrid group commonly cultivated in greenhouses as ornamentals. Its plants have branched flower stems bearing numerous long-lasting flowers, fleshy pseudobulbs and cultivars in many colours.

A small genus of perennial ginger-family plants native to cool forests from the eastern Himalayas through China and Vietnam. The plants die back in winter and reappear in spring, producing yellow or orange summer flowers surrounded by persistent coloured bracts.

A large deciduous hybrid tree most likely formed in Spain or southern France in the 17th century, though a London origin has also been suggested. It has broad, stiff, maple-like leaves and usually pale grey-green bark that peels away. Its tolerance of pollution and compacted soil makes it a popular urban tree.

A genus of bulbous flowering plants distributed from Zimbabwe to South Africa. Its plants have broad leaves and large bulbs usually partly exposed above ground, followed by star-shaped blue flowers and brownish seeds.
A genus of liverworts found mainly in the Northern Hemisphere.
A small genus of three succulent species endemic to coastal South Africa, Namibia and Angola. Its compact triangular leaves form three vertical or spiralling ranks.

A genus of succulent shrubs native to Southern Africa. Its members typically have many long, slender stems that climb or sprawl from a large woody base, along with soft, narrow triangular leaves that clasp the stem.

An orchid subtribe found across the American tropics, from southern Mexico to northern Argentina and Bolivia. Most members grow in shaded, wet lower-canopy settings, either in soil or on often moss-covered trees, and bear one to several spirally arranged flowers from young shoots.

A perennial herb native from Southern Europe through South Asia to Northeast Asia. Its fruit is enclosed by a large, papery orange-to-red covering resembling a lantern. A spreading root system can make it invasive where cultivated.
A monotypic genus of flowering plants native to Burundi, Gabon, Madagascar, Rwanda, Tanzania and the former Zaïre. It contains only Saintpauliopsis lebrunii.
A monotypic genus of flowering plants in the daisy family. Its sole species, Artemisiopsis villosa, is native to eastern and southern Africa.
A genus of flowering plants native to Africa. It belongs to the figwort family and includes species such as Freylinia crispa, Freylinia longiflora and Freylinia tropica.

A genus of short perennial succulents whose native origin is not supplied. The leaves usually form rosettes or spirals and often carry raised white markings, while small, pale, two-lipped flowers appear on tall stalks.

A genus of mosses whose native origin is not supplied. Its upright plants form loose or moderately dense cushions, with narrow leaves held upright or spreading slightly. Spore capsules may sit among the leaves or rise above them.

An evergreen perennial succulent indigenous to South Africa and Lesotho. It is stemless, with dense rosettes of soft, sawtoothed leaves bearing bristly edges and long threadlike tips. Its nectar-rich tubular orange flowers readily attract birds, bees and wasps.

A flowering plant endemic to South Africa’s Cape Province, Dymondia margaretae forms a flat, slow-growing and drought-tolerant carpet. Its leaves curl when water is needed, exposing their silver undersides.
A moss reported as restricted to wooded areas of open grassland in South Africa. However, the variety Oedipodiella australis var. catalaunica is reported from Spain.
A Neotropical subtribe of orchids comprising about 40 genera, including Cattleya, Laelia and Brassavola. Its members may grow in clumps, creep or climb, and may have one or several leaves.

A naturally occurring horsetail hybrid native to Europe and Asia, produced by Equisetum hyemale and Equisetum ramosissimum. It occurs in forests and damp, disturbed places such as clay banks and stream banks.

A naturally occurring oak hybrid native to central and northern Europe, where the ranges of sessile and pedunculate oaks overlap. It is fertile and variable in appearance, generally combining intermediate traits of both parents.

A flowering-plant subtribe whose genera are chiefly native to Africa, with fewer widespread in Arabia and Asia. Most genera are stem succulents that resemble cacti despite not being close relatives. Many have carrion-like flowers that attract flies, although not all smell unpleasant or use flies as pollinators.
A tribe of flowering plants in the sunflower family, with Helenium as its type genus and Gaillardia among its best-known members.

An annual herb native to Europe, from the Mediterranean north to Northern Ireland and Scotland. Its stems and wavy-edged leaves look white and woolly, while dense clusters of pale yellow flowers appear from July to September.

A perennial red seaweed whose attached form is widely distributed on both sides of the North Atlantic. It occurs in attached and drifting forms and can create dense underwater belts that provide spawning habitat for many fish. It is commercially harvested as a source of carrageenan.
edibilityNote: Furcellaran extracted from this seaweed is used to add texture to foods such as sweets, ice cream and puddings.

summary: A plant genus native to eastern Asia, including China, Japan, the Himalayas and Indochina.

A citrus hybrid native from the Philippines through parts of Indonesia, Malaysia and Brunei to Taiwan and tropical southern China. It is a shrub or small tree with winged leaf stalks and white or purplish flowers; its small, round fruit has orange flesh and a very thin ripe peel. The naturally sour fruit is widely used in Philippine condiments, drinks, marinades and preserves.
edibilityNote: The sour fruit and juice are used in condiments, drinks, marinades, preserves and cooked dishes; the peel is sweet.

summary: A perennial flowering hybrid thought to have originated in the Mediterranean region. It grows from underground stems and flowers in mid-to-late spring, with cultivars spanning nearly every colour; some flower again in autumn.

An ornamental hosta of unstated origin, now treated as a cultivar rather than an accepted species. Typical plants have leaves with a broad white centre and green margins, though the centre can narrow or turn greener with time and growing conditions. Tall flower stalks bear pale lavender blossoms attractive to bees.
A genus of flowering succulent plants in the stonecrop family; no native origin is supplied.

A citrus hybrid of unstated native origin, first recorded in Italy in the early 19th century and later widely grown around the Mediterranean. Its sweet fruit is eaten, while oil from the rind flavours food and drinks.
edibilityNote: The sweet fruit is eaten, and rind oil is used to flavour foods and drinks.

summary: A monotypic flowering-plant genus whose sole species is native from southern Europe through South Asia to Northeast Asia. That species is a perennial herb remembered for its large, bright orange-red papery covering around the fruit, resembling a lantern. Its spreading roots can make it invasive.

A bushy shrub hybrid, probably of garden origin. It bears white to rose-pink, urn-shaped flowers in late winter and early spring. Unlike some related plants, it does not require acid soil and is particularly suitable as groundcover.
A tree hybrid growing in the Mediterranean region.
A small genus of flowering plants generally found in the Andes of Colombia, Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia and northwestern Argentina. A cultivated form of Trihesperus latifolius has striped foliage.

A dwarf, perennial bulb native to the mountains of northern Portugal and Spain. It bears small, solitary yellow flowers and needs a cold period to flower. Threatened in the wild, it can nevertheless be cultivated as a cold-hardy garden plant.

A columnar cactus regarded as native to Bolivia and Peru, although widespread cultivation makes its true origins difficult to determine. Its erect stems usually have six to eight ribs, variable needle-like spines, and pale yellow or yellow-green flowers near their tops. Archaeological finds and pre-Columbian objects document human and ritual use over millennia.

A floating freshwater plant originating in tropical and subtropical Mexico, Central America, the Caribbean and South America. Juveniles form flat rosettes with spongy tissue beneath the leaves, while mature plants lift their leaves above the water. It spreads by seeds and broken runner segments and is invasive in Chile.

An herbaceous perennial hybrid documented in the wild in Japan and considered by some to be native there. It spreads by seeds and underground stems, and hairs along the underside leaf vein help distinguish it from both parents. It has a worldwide distribution and is considered invasive in some areas.

A tribe of flowering perennials found mainly in woodland or alpine habitats across temperate North America, Central America and Asia, with one species in South America. They grow from bulbs or underground stems and often have off-white flowers with six petal-like parts. Members produce alkaloids toxic to humans and animals.
edibilityNote: Members produce alkaloids toxic to humans and animals; some are seriously toxic.

summary: A short-stemmed rosette plant native to eastern Africa, from Ethiopia to Malawi. Its thick, spine-tipped leaves are elliptical in cross-section, and it is highly drought tolerant, often growing on dry or rocky ground.

A hybrid flowering plant produced by crossing the common and Spanish bluebells. It spans a broad range of forms between its parents and is widespread along woodland edges and roadsides in Britain and Belgium, particularly in urban areas.

An edible climbing gourd first cultivated in Mesoamerica between southern Mexico and Honduras. Its common fruit is wrinkled and roughly pear-shaped, with mild, watery flesh and one large flattened seed; the roots, stems, seeds and leaves are also edible.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten raw or cooked; roots, stems, seeds and leaves are also edible, with tubers cooked like root vegetables and shoots used in salads or stir-fries.

summary: A garden-raised hybrid shrub first recorded in Northern Ireland by 1951, produced from Berberis oiwakensis and Berberis japonica. Its variable forms are valued for ornamental leaves and winter-long flowering, and many have a striking upright shape.
A branching cactus native to Bolivia. Its light green to bluish stems usually have four to eight ribs, while its fragrant white funnel-shaped flowers open at night.
A columnar cactus native to northwestern Argentina and Bolivia. It has lime-green cylindrical stems with golden spines that fade toward white, and large white flowers that open at night.
A genus of ferns native to the Old World.

A small cactus tribe found mainly in eastern South America, with its greatest diversity in Bolivia, though some members occur farther north and one reaches the Old World. These cacti grow on trees or rocks, taking hanging, creeping or upright forms, and produce fleshy, berry-like fruits.

A shrub or small tree native to southern China and Vietnam. It is endangered in the wild and remembered for waxy yellow flowers, an unusual colour among camellias; the plant has also traditionally been used there to make tea.
edibilityNote: In southern China and Vietnam, the plant has been used to make tea.

summary: A genus of perennial flowering plants native to temperate and subtropical regions worldwide except Australia, New Zealand and Antarctica. They have leaves arising from the base, and most species bear flowers without petals, with coloured sepals providing the display.

Flowering-plant genus native to Asia, ranging through the Himalayas and much of East and Southeast Asia to Sumatra. Cultivated members, called fall-blooming anemones, usually bear white or pink blossoms alongside globe-shaped seed heads from late July to October.
Shrubby flowering-plant genus found in dry parts of the Old World, across regions from southern Africa and the Mediterranean to Central and eastern Asia.
Liverwort genus with a cosmopolitan distribution.
Shrub and subshrub tribe strictly endemic to Australia. Most members are non-aromatic, except the genus Prostanthera, and any hairs are never woolly.

Evergreen flowering climber, a hybrid of Passiflora racemosa and P. caerulea that may have first been made by British nurseryman Thomas Milne in 1819. It has five-lobed leaves, spiral clinging tendrils, and large purple flowers with maroon and white filaments.

Perennial herbaceous hybrid developed at the Royal Horticultural Society's gardens in 1848 from E. japonica and E. vitifolia. It forms large clumps of dark green leaves and bears loose sprays of white, pink, or rose flowers with silky-backed sepals and prominent golden stamens.
Flowering-plant genus native from Assam across temperate eastern Asia and western and central Malesia, and also to the central and eastern United States.

Hybrid fern first found in Mallorca's Sóller Valley and now recorded around the western Mediterranean. Its leathery, plastic-like fronds have a thick, glossy dark-garnet central stem; during dry summer months they dehydrate and appear dead, then quickly green after autumn rain.
Artificial flowering-plant hybrid grown as a shrub or small tree, derived from Hibiscus schizopetalus and the hybrid H. × rosa-sinensis. It apparently has several cultivars.
A green-algal genus with no supplied native range. Its species often form dense green cushions on stones, shells or aquatic plants, and have both attached and upright filaments with blunt tips.
A genus of flowering plants in the arum family, native to tropical northern South America.
A perennial arum native to southern Brazil and Paraguay. It forms dense clumps with glossy, deeply divided green leaves and flowers enclosed by dark red sheaths.

A perennial hybrid aquatic pondweed widespread globally in rivers and lakes, except where water is very soft. Its broad, translucent submerged leaves may be joined by opaque floating leaves, and identification requires a combination of features rather than any single trait.
A small deciduous flowering-tree hybrid originating in Japan but unknown in the wild. Its parents are Prunus itosakura and Prunus incisa.

A cereal hybrid of wheat and rye, first bred in laboratories in late-19th-century Scotland and Germany. It combines wheat's yield and grain quality with rye's tolerance of disease and difficult growing conditions. Although grown mainly for animal feed, its grain is also used in some breakfast cereals and other foods.
edibilityNote: The grain is used less often for human food than animal feed; products include breakfast cereals and foods sold in health-food shops.

summary: A flowering-plant genus native to western and southwestern Europe and Morocco. It contains only one species, Trocdaris verticillata.

A genus of tropical and subtropical woody flowering plants whose ten species range from southeastern Mexico through Central America to northwestern South America and several Caribbean islands. Some species are grown for their ornamental flowers.

A natural pitcher-plant hybrid known only from Mount Kinabalu and nearby Mount Tambuyukon on Borneo. Its pitchers vary from yellow to scarlet and combine features of both parents, with raised inner ribs ending in elongated teeth.
A shrubby hybrid of unstated native origin, arising between Cistus albidus and Cistus crispus. It has grey-green leaves and pink to purple flowers.

A semideciduous hybrid tree arising naturally in southwestern Europe where its parents, Turkey oak and cork oak, occur together. Named cultivars are widely grown in gardens, parks and tree collections.

An evergreen hybrid subshrub of unstated native origin, derived from Pavonia makoyana and Pavonia multiflora. Its unusual purple-grey flowers sit within bright red outer floral structures and appear in late summer.
A cactus genus native to Bolivia and Argentina. Its plants are usually solitary, with rounded to oblong stems and flowers ranging from golden yellow and orange to reddish yellow near the stem tips.

A group of hybrid evergreen shrubs first bred in Cornwall from Camellia saluenensis and Camellia japonica, with no wild native origin stated. The group flowers abundantly, and nearly all crosses have translucent petals; some varieties bloom for several months.

An artificial flowering-plant hybrid of unstated geographic origin, derived from Begonia socotrana and the hybrid Begonia × tuberhybrida. It typically has doubled flowers in every colour except blue and can bloom through autumn and winter, sometimes nearly year-round.

A genus of flowering plants native across Southeast Asia, the Indian Subcontinent, southern China, Tibet, Taiwan, Japan, Papuasia and Australia. Its members commonly range from scrambling subshrubs to small trees, with many growing on other plants or as vines.

A naturally occurring terrestrial orchid hybrid distributed in Sardinia and Mallorca, in moist, partly shaded woodland. It flowers early in March and has a large dark brown, sometimes nearly black, lip marked centrally with a silver H and edged with lighter velvety hairs.
A flowering-plant species native to western and southwestern Europe and Morocco. It is the sole species in the genus Trocdaris.

A perennial succulent hybrid developed in France, it forms basal offsets and may have little or no stem. Its blue-green, paddle-shaped leaves develop orange or pink edges in strong sunlight, while numerous small flowers are bright yellow and pink.

A thorny citrus hybrid probably originating in India, it bears irregular fruit with orange flesh and peel at maturity. Its abundant juice is very acidic and used for seasoning or drinks, while the aromatic leaves are also used as seasoning.
edibilityNote: The acidic juice is used for seasoning and drinks; the aromatic leaves are also used as seasoning.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree native mainly to highland Colombia, southern Brazil and northeastern Uruguay, and also found in eastern Paraguay and northern Argentina. Its green autumn fruit has juicy, sweet-tart, strongly aromatic flesh; the edible pulp is commonly scooped from the halved fruit, and the flower petals are edible too.
edibilityNote: The skin and flower petals are edible; fruit pulp is eaten raw and used in desserts or salads.

summary: A deciduous large shrub or small tree native to the southeastern Balkans, Asia Minor, the Caucasus, Crimea and northern Iran, and possibly Turkmenistan. Its reddish-brown fruit becomes edible after frost or storage softens it through “bletting,” producing wrinkled dark skin and an interior resembling apple sauce.
edibilityNote: Bletted fruit is eaten raw, sometimes with sugar and cream, or made into jelly and medlar cheese.

summary: An annual legume domesticated in the Fertile Crescent of the Near East, it is grown for its edible, lens-shaped seeds. The pods usually contain two seeds, which are eaten worldwide, especially in soups, stews and thick curries such as dal.
edibilityNote: Seeds are commonly boiled for soups, stews and curries, but may also be soaked, sprouted, fried or baked.

summary: An artificial perennial aquatic hybrid naturalised in Indian lakes in Meghalaya and Jammu and Kashmir, it grows from a horizontal underground stem. Its unmottled leaves are bronze when young, and it produces small red flowers but is sterile.
A commonly cultivated aloe hybrid probably developed in Europe from cultivated plants, rather than arising in its South African parents’ wild habitat. It has become naturalised in parts of Portugal.

A section of grasses native mainly to Atlantic coasts in Europe, Africa, the Americas and southern Atlantic islands, with limited occurrences on western North American coasts and inland American freshwater habitats. Its species often form large, dense, fast-growing colonies in coastal salt marshes, and many can hybridise when they meet.

An artificial perennial aquatic hybrid naturalised in Australia, New Zealand, North America and Europe, it grows in ponds, lakes and canals. Its floating leaves have reddish-brown marbling above and purple spots below, while its large daytime flowers are often fragrant and white, faintly pink or yellow. It is generally sterile but spreads through creeping stems and can densely cover ponds.
A small genus of flowering cacti native to southern Brazil. Its species grow as epiphytes on trees and have flowers with a short tube where the petals join at the base.

A cultivar group of flowering hybrids derived from three species from Chile and Argentina. These soft-stemmed plants bear yellow to red flowers, dislike summer heat and rarely bloom again indoors without greenhouse-like humidity.

A flowering hybrid between Viola cornuta and the hybrid pansy Viola × wittrockiana. It has wider, slightly overlapping petals, while perennial growth, scented flowers or a longer spur may distinguish it from the latter parent.
A leggy hybrid shrub or small tree developed from cherry plum and sand cherry. Its strong-tasting fruit is eaten and made into jams or preserves, but eating the pits is not advised.
edibilityNote: Strong-tasting fruits are eaten or made into jams and preserves; eating the pits is not advised.

summary: An evergreen hybrid shrub with no native origin supplied. Its dark green leaves have silvery, scaly undersides, and small fragrant white flowers appear in autumn.

A cultivated deciduous hybrid shrub, absent from the wild and probably originating in the foothills of central Asia or Iran. Its fragrant pink to light-red flowers are harvested for rose oil and rose water; the edible petals flavor foods, garnish dishes, make tea and are preserved in sugar.
edibilityNote: Petals are used as flavoring, garnish and herbal tea, or preserved in sugar; rose water and powdered roses also feature in cooking.

summary: A terrestrial natural orchid hybrid found in Italy, especially Tuscany. It grows in meadows and open ground in sun or partial shade, producing dense cones of small pink, spotted flowers from April to June.
An artificial flowering-plant hybrid between Freesia corymbosa and Freesia leichtlinii subsp. alba; no native origin or other features are supplied.
A genus of 73 flowering-plant species distributed across Europe, northern Africa, the Middle East and central Asia.

A genus of 43 flowering plants in the pea family, native across the Americas from the United States to southern Argentina and Uruguay. Some species are called mesquites, and tannins occur mainly in their bark and wood, with low concentrations in the pods.
An ornamental small-tree hybrid that arose between cultivated hawthorns. It has glossy, dark green, unlobed leaves.

A succulent flowering plant native to the Sierra Madre Oriental of northeastern Mexico. Its long green leaves tend to curl and have minute edge teeth but no pointed terminal spine; white or pale-yellow flowers crowd the upper part of a short spike.

A perennial group of flowering hybrids of garden origin, created by crosses between Heuchera and Tiarella. Its plants are notable for colourful, patterned leaves and white, pink or cream flowers that usually appear in spring.

An annual flowering plant native to North Africa, Europe and parts of Asia. It has four-petalled yellow flowers followed by beaked pods, while its dark brown to black seeds are commonly used as a spice.
edibilityNote: Seeds are used as a spice; young leaves, buds and flowers are edible, and shoots and leaves are eaten cooked in Ethiopia.

summary: A flowering grass hybrid native to mainland Portugal.
A group of small hybrid succulents produced by crossing Pachyphytum and Echeveria. The plants can develop compact, low forms in sunny conditions and can be propagated from detached top rosettes.

A tropical tree native to the Indian subcontinent, southern China and mainland Southeast Asia. Its aromatic leaves season many South and Southeast Asian dishes; its shiny black fruits have sweet edible pulp, but the seeds may be toxic.
edibilityNote: Fresh leaves are used in South and Southeast Asian cooking; berry pulp is edible, but the seeds may be toxic to humans.

summary: A flowering plant in the asparagus family, recorded from Portugal's Madeira Archipelago.
An evergreen tree from South Africa and Mozambique, with male and female reproductive structures on separate trees. Its fruit is edible.
edibilityNote: The fruit is edible.

summary: A shrubby hybrid rose of cultivated Dutch origin, developed between the 17th and 19th centuries, possibly earlier. Its highly scented flowers are round and densely packed with thin overlapping petals, usually pink but sometimes white or dark red-purple.

A citrus tree whose wild form evolved in a restricted region of southern China and Vietnam. Its small, flattened fruits have thin, loose, pebbly skin and separate easily into segments; most commercial strains are sweeter than the bitter ancestral mandarin.
edibilityNote: Fruit is eaten fresh or used in salads, desserts and main dishes; peel is used fresh, as zest, dried, or as flavouring.

summary: An evergreen shrub or small tree of cultivated west Pacific origin, created by Polynesians from parent species originating in Vanuatu and French Polynesia. Its typically red, five-petalled flowers have prominent orange-tipped structures, while cultivated forms range from white and yellow to blue and purple and may be double-flowered.
edibilityNote: Flowers are eaten in salads in the Pacific Islands and are dried for beverages in several countries.

summary: A rosette-forming flowering plant endemic to Puebla and Oaxaca, Mexico. Its thick, pointed oval leaves are olive, grey or whitish green with red-brown markings, and its late-spring flowers are scarlet with yellow tips.
A grass native to the Pyrenees of France and Spain, Portugal and Morocco. It is the only species in its genus and has blunt to squared-off outer flower bracts, with florets about half their length.
A genus of four grass species native to Mediterranean Europe, North Africa and western Asia from the Levant to Turkmenistan.

An annual or perennial herb or woody-based subshrub, likely native to West Africa. Its pale flowers have a dark red spot, while the calyx becomes fleshy and deep crimson as the fruit matures. The calyces are commonly steeped for an infusion, and the stems yield fibre.
edibilityNote: Leaves, young stems and fruits are cooked; calyces and fruits make drinks, and the fruits can be made into jam.

It usually grows in acidic forests on soil near tree bases, sheltered banks or rocks. In Tunisia it was sterile and confined to a tiny patch in the Oued Zen Valley.

An annual tuft-forming grass widespread in Eurasia, although the sources do not explicitly identify its native range. Its narrow flower head usually arches downward, with its lower part often enclosed by the uppermost leaf sheath; the blue-green plant soon turns straw-yellow.

sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

Along the Pacific coast it characteristically grows on soil banks in redwood forests, while other habitats include wet, shaded banks and overturned tree bases.

sources.title: Epipterygium tozeri in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

Pacific and Atlantic populations may be distinct, and the species could include several unrecognised taxa.

sources.title: Salicornia depressa in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

sources.title: Stokesia in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A genus of flowering plants found in the Neotropics, with most of its roughly fifteen species concentrated in Brazil and a few elsewhere in Central and South America.

sources.title: Ptychomitrium in Moss Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: An almost cosmopolitan genus of mosses whose native origin is not supplied. Its small plants often form dense, lime-encrusted cushions or tufa, with leaves clustered in whorls and distinctively toothed near the base.

sources.title: Eucladium in Bryophyte Flora of North America @ efloras.org
sources.attribution: Bryophyte Flora of North America, eFloras

sources.title: Lescuraea in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

sources.title: Anoectangium aestivum in Moss Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A mat-forming moss of unspecified native origin, found on logs, tree bases, soil and rocks in forests at low to moderate elevations. It has concave leaves, curved nearly upright capsules and short-tapered, sword-shaped branches that are somewhat flattened.

sources.title: Callicladium haldaneanum in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: An annual plant of unspecified native origin. A Catalan account places it in small grasslands dominated by annual plants.

sources.title: Fissidens asplenioides in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

sources.title: Grimmia lisae in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

sources.title: Hedwigia stellata in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

sources.title: Tortella flavovirens in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

sources.title: Laurencia obtusa (Hudson) J.V. Lamouroux — Seaweed.ie, Michael D. Guiry

sources.title: Lomentaria orcadensis (Harvey) F.S. Collins ex W.R. Taylor — Seaweed.ie, Michael D. Guiry

summary: A biennial or subshrub native to the western and southern Balkan Peninsula, growing mainly in the temperate biome.

sources.title: Verbascum undulatum Lam. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A genus of relatively large plants forming coarse mats, with no native origin supplied. Its yellow-green to brown growth has feather-like stems and broad, pointed, finely toothed leaves with either no central vein or a short, double one.

sources.title: Nogopterium in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A tuberous perennial native from Zimbabwe to South Africa, primarily growing in subtropical environments.

sources.title: Gloriosa modesta (Hook.) J.C.Manning & Vinn. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A succulent perennial native to southern tropical and southern Africa, primarily found in deserts or dry shrubland.

sources.title: Bulbine latifolia (L.f.) Spreng. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A moss of unspecified native origin, usually dark red to red-green and sometimes purple-black. Its tightly overlapping leaves and stems have a metallic sheen, and it grows on damp or wet silica-rich rock and nearby soil, often around waterfalls or springs.

sources.title: Imbribryum miniatum in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A deciduous shrub of unspecified native origin that may grow upright or climb. Its non-fragrant white flowers appear after the leaves, followed by compressed, egg-shaped fruit that ripens red.

sources.title: Viburnum foetidum in Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A red seaweed of unspecified native origin, forming leathery tufts that range from brownish red to dark purple or black and may bleach brown in summer. Its highly variable branches arise above a tough, flexible, branch-free base, and it tolerates substrates ranging from pebbles and bedrock to marina pontoons.

sources.title: Black siphon weed (Vertebrata fucoides) - MarLIN - The Marine Life Information Network

summary: A shrub or tree native from Bolivia to Brazil and northern Argentina, primarily growing in seasonally dry tropical environments.

sources.title: Vassobia breviflora (Sendtn.) Hunz. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: An aquatic perennial native to Cambodia, the Philippines, New Guinea through northern Australia, and New Caledonia, primarily growing in wet tropical environments.

sources.title: Vallisneria nana R.Br. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A seaweed of unspecified native origin, with a thin blade rising from a disc-shaped attachment and dividing irregularly into forks, often from the margins. It grows on rocks or other plants and is rarely found on the shore but occurs below low tide to depths of 30 metres.
A shrub native to Daitojima in the Nansei Islands and the Ogasawara Islands, primarily growing in subtropical environments.

sources.title: Zanthoxylum beecheyanum K.Koch — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A shrub found in mountain forests of central Taiwan. Its young shoots have dense, coarse red-brown hairs, while its pink, funnel-shaped flowers bear darker pink flecks.

sources.title: Rhododendron rubropilosum in Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A low deciduous shrub found in Taiwan’s open grasslands. It has small, stiff leaves and red to dark purple funnel-shaped flowers with protruding stamens; the account’s authors had seen no specimens themselves.

sources.title: Rhododendron noriakianum in Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A climbing shrub native to Taiwan, including forests and mountain slopes on the Hengchun Peninsula. Its four-sided branches have rings of long hairs at the nodes, and it produces nearly spherical berries.

sources.title: Medinilla formosana in Flora of China @ efloras.org
Medinilla formosana Hayata — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A low, spreading, semi-evergreen shrub native to Taiwan. It has thick, leathery leaves, solitary white flowers and red oval fruits, and grows in sunny rocky high-mountain habitats.

sources.title: Cotoneaster morrisonensis in Flora of China @ efloras.org
Cotoneaster morrisonensis Hayata — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A temperate plant native to the northwestern North Island of New Zealand.

sources.title: Veronica macrocarpa Vahl — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A shrub found in Taiwan’s mountain forests and slopes. Its young branches are densely hairy, its leaves have pale, hairy undersides and sharply toothed edges, and its upright leafy shoots carry large, many-flowered terminal clusters.

sources.title: Spiraea formosana in Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A seaweed with no native origin supplied. It grows around the high-water mark on muddy British and Irish shores, often attached to the lower stems of saltmarsh flowering plants, and can be locally abundant.

sources.title: Bostrychia scorpioides (Hudson) Montagne ex Kützing — Seaweed.ie, Michael D. Guiry

summary: A seaweed with no native origin supplied. Its thin, single-layered fronds range from olive-green to brown-purple or blackish and hang from rocks on sandy, semi-exposed shores; it is most common in spring and early summer.
A perennial plant with underground stems, native to Madeira. It grows primarily in the subtropical biome.

sources.title: Semele menezesii J.G.Costa — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A seaweed with no native origin supplied. It has firm, fleshy, flattened dark-red fronds with repeated forks, often paler blunt tips and irregularly sculpted edges; reproductive growths resemble external warts.

sources.title: Gymnogongrus crenulatus J. Agardh — Seaweed.ie, Michael D. Guiry

summary: A plant species native to Mozambique, growing mainly in seasonally dry tropical areas.

sources.title: Aloe ribauensis T.A.McCoy, Rulkens & O.J.Baptista — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A liverwort of unspecified native origin, associated locally with sheltered, acidic places in rainy areas and oceanic oakwoods. It is relatively large, yellow-brown and untidy-looking, with loose leaf lobes and an often recurved upper lobe.

A seaweed of unspecified native origin that forms dense, brownish-red, tassel-like tufts of lightly branched hair-like filaments. It grows on limpets along exposed shores and sometimes on Codium fragile in the lower intertidal zone.

sources.title: Colaconema caespitosum (J. Agardh) Jackelman, Stegenga & Bolton — Seaweed.ie, Michael D. Guiry

summary: An annual or perennial plant native to central and eastern Spain, growing mainly in the temperate biome.

sources.title: Ionopsidium glastifolium (L.) M.Koch — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A plant of unspecified native origin, found locally in humid western woodlands and sheltered, north-facing rocky places. It has conspicuous, relatively sparse teeth along the leaf margins and can be difficult to distinguish from Plagiochila bifaria without microscopic examination.
A perennial plant native to Madeira, growing mainly in the temperate biome.

sources.title: Viola sequeirae Capelo, R.Jardim, J.C.Costa, Lousã & Rivas Mart. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A perennial plant native to the Mediterranean region, growing mainly in the subtropical biome.

sources.title: Oloptum thomasii (Duby) Banfi & Galasso — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A fern of unspecified native origin, recorded in lower mountain areas of southeastern Taiwan and parts of southern Asia, Japan, Africa and Indonesia. It has a short upright rhizome with brown hairy scales and clustered, lance-shaped fronds that are deep green when dry and hairy on both surfaces.

sources.title: Leptogramma pozoi in Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: An annual plant native from Macaronesia and the Mediterranean region eastward to the Caucasus, growing mainly in the temperate biome.

sources.title: Vicia lentoides (Ten.) Coss. & Germ. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A winter annual or biennial native to South America and introduced widely elsewhere. It has basal leaves that remain as a rosette during flowering, with white-felted undersides, and dense flower-head arrays that later become branched and interrupted.

sources.title: Gamochaeta impatiens in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A small alga whose native origin is not supplied. It grows in upright tufts with whorled branches and lives attached to animals or other plants from the lower shore to shallow water.
A shrub or tree native from western South America to Venezuela. It grows mainly in wet tropical environments and is used medicinally.

sources.title: Varronia cylindristachya Ruiz & Pav. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: An annual plant native from Portugal to southern Italy and northwestern Africa. It grows mainly in temperate environments.

sources.title: Avena castellana (Romero Zarco) Romero Zarco & L.Sáez — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: An annual plant native to the Mediterranean and La Gomera in the Canary Islands. It grows mainly in subtropical environments.

sources.title: Avena hirtula Lag. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A red-to-brown alga native to Asia and the Indo-Pacific and introduced in Europe and northwestern North America. Its fine, irregularly branching stems intertwine into pom-poms and can form dense mats on rocks, mussels, other algae or gravel.

A genus of three annual plants from the western Mediterranean basin. Its flowers have two stamens, making the genus easy to recognize within its group. Fruit shape varies markedly within each species, while flower colour and shape help distinguish the three species.

A perennial succulent native to the Tehuacán-Cuicatlán region of Puebla in southern Mexico, where it grows in semi-desert. Its creeping or cascading fleshy stems carry rosettes of thick, waxy green to grey-green leaves, often tinged purple. Small pale pink to purple star-shaped flowers appear in spring or summer.
A scrambling shrub native to western Europe, growing mainly in the temperate biome.

sources.title: Rubus elegantispinosus (A.Schumach.) H.E.Weber — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A temperate plant native from the Cape Province through Lesotho to KwaZulu-Natal.

sources.title: Cotula lineariloba (DC.) Hilliard — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A genus of flowering plants native from Mozambique to southern Africa. It contains only one known species, Helichrysopsis septentrionalis.

sources.title: Helichrysopsis Kirp. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A section of plants within the genus Dendrobium, found from India east to New Guinea and Australia and north to Japan and Korea. Its plants have slender, moderately long pseudobulbs, with leaves along their upper two-thirds.

An evergreen hybrid shrub of garden origin, derived from Holantarctic Veronica elliptica and New Zealand Veronica speciosa. It has glossy dark-green leaves and dense clusters of blue-violet flowers with white throats. It tolerates salt spray and wind but is vulnerable to hard frost, especially inland.

sources.title: VERONICA ×FRANCISCANA  (Eastw.) J. T. Howell, P. H. Raven et P. Rubtzoff – rozrazil / veronika | BOTANY.cz

summary: A dark red seaweed native to the northwestern Pacific. It may form large mats, growing either as bushy clumps or long, irregularly branched strands whose hollow sections can feel elastic. It favours sheltered muddy waters such as bays, harbours and estuaries.

sources.title: Gracilaria vermiculophylla (Ohmi) Papenfuss, 1967 — National Museums Northern Ireland, Habitas

summary: A marine alga with no native origin stated. Its upright growth forms dense tufts, with rootlike filaments creating a thick outer layer. It grows on other plants, animals or rock along the lower shore.

sources.title: Callithamnion granulatum (Ducluzeau) C Agardh — National Museums Northern Ireland, Habitas

summary: An evergreen tree native to central China, chiefly along the Yangtze River. Its crown has strongly drooping branches: young trees are narrow and pointed, while older trees develop a broader, eventually flattened crown. The brown bark becomes divided into short, irregular yellow-brown strips.
edibilityNote: In its homeland, branches are used to smoke pork and the ash to pickle duck eggs.

summary: A succulent with no explicitly stated native origin, occurring in central and southern Europe, especially the Alps and western Balkans. It is a hardy, prolific plant of dry, stony limestone ground, with stronger and less trailing growth than Petrosedum montanum.
A flowering orchid endemic to the island of São Tomé.

A seaweed with no native origin stated. It grows on rock, sending creeping stems through sponges and soft rock from the lower shore into waters about 25 metres deep. Around Britain and Ireland it is widespread but uncommon.

sources.title: Rhodymenia holmesii Ardissone — Seaweed.ie, Michael D. Guiry

summary: A red alga with no native origin stated. Its upright cylindrical fronds branch irregularly at very narrow angles and end in rounded tips; the cells are large enough to see unaided. It is recorded as very rare on submerged rock in shallow water.

sources.title: Bornetia secundiflora (J Agardh) Thuret — National Museums Northern Ireland, Habitas

summary: A marine alga with no native origin stated. It grows upright with a cylindrical form and dense, overlapping rings of divided branches. It occurs on rock in lower-shore pools and underwater.

sources.title: Halurus equisetifolius (Lightfoot) Kützing — National Museums Northern Ireland, Habitas

summary: A calcareous alga with no native origin stated. It forms either a thin hard crust on firm surfaces or loose, fragile branched nodules that can gather into dense gravel-like beds. Living plants are reddish to deep pink with a violet tinge, turning white after death.

sources.title: Boreolithothamnion glaciale nodules amongst pebbles with the sunstar Crossaster papposus, Isle of Lewis. — MarLIN, Marine Biological Association

summary: An epiphytic subshrub native to tropical Africa, growing mainly in wet tropical habitats.

sources.title: Tridactyle tridactylites (Rolfe) Schltr. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A riverside moss with no native origin stated. When wet, its tongue-shaped leaves show thickened, scalloped borders; older leaves often split neatly into rectangular fragments.
An annual plant native to the Canary Islands and from the western Mediterranean east to western Italy, growing mainly in subtropical regions.

sources.title: Festuca alopecuros Schousb. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A temperate plant native to Portugal.

sources.title: Centaurea francoi Figueiredo & Gideon F.Sm. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A herbaceous perennial hybrid with no native origin stated. It forms fast-growing arching clumps and has flowers in many solid or two-toned colors, sometimes with ruffled or patterned edges.

sources.title: Daylily - Hemerocallis hybrida | North Carolina Extension Gardener Plant Toolbox
sources.attribution: North Carolina State University Extension Plant Toolbox

summary: A tuber-forming plant native from western Portugal to western and southwestern Spain, growing mainly in temperate regions.

sources.title: Crocus clusii J.Gay — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A climbing, tuber-forming plant native to Madeira and the Canary Islands, growing mainly in subtropical regions.

sources.title: Dioscorea edulis (Lowe) M.Campos, Wilkin & Viruel — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A fully parasitic plant native to the Canary Islands and western Mediterranean, growing mainly in subtropical regions.

sources.title: Orobanche castellana Reut. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A short-rhizomed plant recorded from western and central Europe east to central Siberia, with no explicitly stated native origin. Its much-branched, deeply grooved solid stem bears twice-divided basal leaves whose lowest leaflet pair is conspicuously unequal.

sources.title: LIBANOTIS PYRENAICA (L.) Bourgeau – žebřice pyrenejská / rebrica pyrenejská | BOTANY.cz

summary: A genus of herbs, undershrubs and shrubs widely distributed across the Old and New Worlds. Its leaves range from a single leaflet to feather-like arrangements, while flowers may stand alone or form varied clusters and range from violet or purple to white or pale yellow.

sources.title: Astragalus in Flora of Pakistan @ efloras.org

summary: A genus of shrubs, sometimes trees or vines, occurring in the southeastern United States, Cuba and eastern Asia. Its evergreen or deciduous leaves are often toothed, and its clustered white, urn-shaped flowers are followed by dry capsules containing many seeds.

sources.title: Pieris in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A perennial evergreen genus native to the southeastern United States and introduced elsewhere. Its leaves have two hinged lobes edged with stout bristles; three trigger hairs on each inner surface cause the trap to snap shut when properly stimulated.

sources.title: Dionaea in Flora of North America @ efloras.org
Dionaea J.Ellis — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A genus of aromatic, gland-covered herbs, subshrubs and shrubs, widely distributed and especially associated with western North America. Male and female flower heads are separate but often occur on the same plant, with female heads developing spiny-tipped coverings around the fruits.

sources.title: Ambrosia in Trees and shrubs of the Andes of Ecuador @ efloras.org
sources.attribution: Trees and shrubs of the Andes of Ecuador, eFloras

summary: A genus of mostly perennial herbs found mainly in Asia and Europe, with one species in North America and a few in East Africa. Many species are robust and tall, bearing broad-based compound leaves and spreading umbrella-shaped clusters of mostly white flowers.

sources.title: Heracleum in Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A genus of annual, occasionally perennial herbs from Eurasia and northern Africa, introduced nearly worldwide. Its yellow flowers form clusters that lengthen as fruits develop, and its pods have a seed-bearing section plus a terminal section that may be seedless or hold one or two seeds.

sources.title: Sinapis in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A genus of perennial evergreen, mat-forming herbs from tropical Africa, Asia, Australia and Polynesia, introduced in North America. Stout creeping underground stems produce crowded, firm basal leaves, while the flowers are followed by long-lasting blue to bluish-purple berries.

sources.title: Dianella in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A genus of annual or perennial herbs, subshrubs and shrubs distributed through the tropics and subtropics of both hemispheres, with about two-thirds of its species restricted to the Americas. Most are hairy, with alternate leaves and flowers ranging from yellow or white to pink or orange.

sources.title: Sida in Flora of Pakistan @ efloras.org

summary: A very small moss found in China, India, Japan and Africa, where it grows on rocks. It forms dense tufts containing both fertile and sterile stems, with narrow pointed leaves and upright cylindrical capsules.

sources.title: Fissidens curvatus in Moss Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A moss species recorded reproducing in Sweden and classified as endangered in Finland. It inhabits limestone cliffs and limestone quarries.
A liverwort species of unstated native origin, blue crystalwort is recorded across Europe, Africa, Australia and both North and South America.
A tree genus native to Africa, Tamarindus has one species and is widely cultivated across the tropics. It has paired leaflets, small flower clusters and pods with thick pulp surrounding the seeds.

sources.title: Tamarindus in Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A moss genus of unstated native origin, Ditrichum occurs on every continent, including maritime Antarctica, from near sea level to mountain regions. Its plants form green to yellow-green tufts, and their capsules typically have 16 teeth split into threadlike segments.

sources.title: Ditrichum in Bryophyte Flora of North America @ efloras.org
sources.attribution: Bryophyte Flora of North America, eFloras

summary: A mostly perennial herb genus of unstated native origin, Cota occurs in Europe, southwestern Asia and northern Africa; its North American representative is introduced. It typically has upright stems, deeply divided leaves and flower heads with yellow rays surrounding many small central flowers.

sources.title: Cota in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A moss genus of unstated native origin, Racomitrium occurs across much of the world, including Antarctica. Its coarse, rigid plants are usually greyish or brownish, with many short side branches and leaves ending in long, pale, rough-edged points. The fruiting stalks have a uniquely roughened surface among upright mosses.

sources.title: Racomitrium in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A genus of annual or perennial herbs of unstated native origin, Glycine occurs across tropical, subtropical and temperate parts of the Eastern Hemisphere. Its members may twine, climb, creep or stand erect, usually bearing root nodules and leaves divided into three leaflets. Their pods split open and the valves coil afterward.

sources.title: Glycine in Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A genus of perennial herbs of unstated native origin, Gloriosa occurs in southern and tropical Africa and tropical Asia. Its elongated stems often climb using tendrils at the leaf tips, while the large, showy flowers have six spreading or swept-back segments. The seeds have bright red, spongy coats.

sources.title: Gloriosa in Flora of China @ efloras.org

summary: A moss genus of unstated native origin, Gymnostomum occurs worldwide except Antarctica and favors moist, lime-rich environments. It forms green turf or cushions, with leaves that spread outward when moist but draw inward when dry. Its capsules lack teeth around their openings.

sources.title: Gymnostomum in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A shrub native to tropical and subtropical America, shrubby Indian mallow grows mainly in seasonally dry tropical areas and open, arid habitats. It has roughly hairy stems and leaves, with orange-yellow flowers appearing throughout the year.

sources.title: Abutilon abutiloides in Flora of North America @ efloras.org
Abutilon abutiloides (Jacq.) Garcke ex Hochr. — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A climbing shrub or liana native to southwestern Texas, sevenleaf creeper is endemic to the Edwards Plateau and Lampasas Cut Plain. Its leaves usually have seven thick, glossy leaflets, while its branched tendrils lack adhesive discs. It bears greenish to reddish-green flowers followed by rounded berries.

sources.title: Parthenocissus heptaphylla in Flora of North America @ efloras.org
Parthenocissus heptaphylla (Planch.) Britton — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A leafy moss species of unspecified native origin, Small Twisted Moss is usually dull dark green or yellow-green above and brown to black below. Its leaves curl or twist when dry and spread when moist, while its well-developed reproductive teeth are conspicuously twisted.

sources.title: Tortella humilis in Flora of North America @ efloras.org

summary: A shrub or tree native from Mexico to Honduras, the Caribbean to Venezuela, and eastern Brazil, desert senna grows mainly in wet tropical regions.

sources.title: Senna polyphylla (Jacq.) H.S.Irwin & Barneby — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A tree genus distributed chiefly in the Old World tropics, Pterygota has usually unlobed, heart-shaped leaves. Its flowers lack petals, and its woody, nearly spherical fruits contain numerous seeds, each with a long or broad blade-shaped wing.

sources.title: Pterygota in Flora of Pakistan @ efloras.org

summary: An annual native to Madeira and the Canary Islands, Luzula elegans is restricted there to Madeira Island and the islands of Gran Canaria, Tenerife, La Gomera, El Hierro and La Palma.

sources.title: Luzula elegans Lowe — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew

summary: A perennial hybrid native from the Caucasus through Central Asia and Iran, Sand Lucerne grows mainly in temperate regions. It is the hybrid of Medicago falcata and Medicago sativa.

sources.title: Medicago × varia Martyn — Plants of the World Online
sources.attribution: Plants of the World Online, Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew
